items.readable_text:
Content:
We always introduce errors in our measurements whenever we round or approximate numbers. In this lesson, we will explore how to quantify and describe measurement errors.

Content:
Suppose that a particular rope measures precisely [MATH: 48.9\,\textrm{cm}.] Now, imagine we take a meterstick and record a measurement of [MATH: 50\,\textrm{cm}] to the nearest [MATH: 10] centimeters. Let's mark this approximation on our meterstick.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/54f7538c31e487c9f72f2300e56958ae]

Content:
The error of a measurement equals the difference between the rounded estimate and the "true" value. So, in this example, the error of our approximation equals

Content:
[MATH: 50\,\textrm{cm} - 48.9\,\textrm{cm} = 1.1\textrm{cm}.]

Content:
We often don't know the "true" measurement in practical problems. So, the next best thing is to determine a lower bound and an upper bound for our measurement:

Content:
- The lower bound of a measurement is its smallest possible value.
- The upper bound of a measurement is its largest possible value.

Content:
Let's figure out the lower and upper bounds of our [MATH: 50\,\textrm{cm}] approximation:

Content:
- The lower bound is [MATH: 45 \, \textrm{cm}] because this is the smallest value that gives [MATH: 50 \, \textrm{cm}] when rounded to the nearest [MATH: 10\,\textrm{cm}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7dab97aad62154d948e83335d34810d9]

Content:
- The upper bound is [MATH: 55 \, \textrm{cm}] because this is (almost) the largest value that gives [MATH: 50 \, \textrm{cm}] when rounded to the nearest [MATH: 10\,\textrm{cm}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f234ca2c55e545b2e751312d704ba3c2]

Content:
Let's use the letter [MATH: l] to denote the "true" length of the rope. Then, we can combine our lower and upper bound measurements into a single statement, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 45\,\textrm{cm} \leq l \lt 55\,\textrm{cm}]

Content:
Notice that we used a strict "<" inequality for the upper bound. We cannot include [MATH: 55\textrm{cm}] in our set of values because this number rounds to [MATH: 60\,\textrm{cm},] not [MATH: 50\,\textrm{cm}].

Content:
We can visualize the lower and upper bounds on our diagram as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f62fde44578ca41f2b28f7bf61145112]

• The lower and upper bound depend on our approximation's degree of accuracy.

  • In the last example, the degree of accuracy was [MATH: 10\,\textrm{cm}] because the rope was measured to the nearest [MATH: 10] centimeters.

  • If we change the degree of accuracy, the lower and upper bounds will also change. So, for example, if we measured the rope to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{cm},] the lower and upper bounds would be different.

  • The greatest possible error is the largest amount the "true" value can be from the approximation.

  • This greatest possible error is always one-half of the degree of accuracy. So, in the last example, the greatest possible error in our measurement was

- The greatest possible error is the largest amount the "true" value can be from the approximation.
- This greatest possible error is always one-half of the degree of accuracy. So, in the last example, the greatest possible error in our measurement was

sections.readable_text: [MATH: \dfrac{10\,\textrm{cm}}{2} = {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}}.]

sections.normalized_html:
• To compute the lower bound of an approximation, we subtract the greatest possible error from the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have [MATH: \textrm{lower bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} - {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 45\,\textrm{cm.}]

  • To compute the upper bound of an approximation, we add the greatest possible error to the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have [MATH: \textrm{upper bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} + {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 55\,\textrm{cm.}]

sections.normalized_html: The height [MATH: h] of a lamppost is [MATH: 30\,\textrm{ft}] to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ft}.] Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.
sections.readable_text: The height [MATH: h] of a lamppost is [MATH: 30\,\textrm{ft}] to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ft}.] Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Our measurement is given to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ft}.] So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

[MATH: \dfrac{1\,\textrm{ft}}{2} = 0.5\,\textrm{ft}.]

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

[MATH: lower bound|= 30ft − 0.5ft; = 29.5ft; upper bound|= 30ft + 0.5ft; = 30.5ft]

Since the exact value of [MATH: h] lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

[MATH: 29.5\,\textrm{ft} \leq h < 30.5\,\textrm{ft}.]

sections.normalized_html: The dimensions of a parking lot are [MATH: 90\, \textrm{m} \times 50\, \textrm{m}], where each dimension is measured to the nearest [MATH: 10\, \textrm{m}.] Rounded to the nearest ten square meters, what is the upper bound for the area of the parking lot?
sections.readable_text: The dimensions of a parking lot are [MATH: 90\, \textrm{m} \times 50\, \textrm{m}], where each dimension is measured to the nearest [MATH: 10\, \textrm{m}.] Rounded to the nearest ten square meters, what is the upper bound for the area of the parking lot?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Each dimension is given to the nearest [MATH: 10\,\textrm{m}.] So, the greatest possible error of these measurements is

[MATH: \dfrac{10\,\textrm{m}}{2} = 5\,\textrm{m}.]

We wish to find the upper bound for the area of the parking lot. Therefore, we require the upper bound of each dimension.

The upper bounds for each dimension are as follows:

[MATH: 90m + 5m = 95m; 50m + 5m = 55m]

So, the upper bound for the area of the parking lot is

[MATH: A|= 95m × 55m; = 5225; ≈ 5230m^{2},]

rounded to the nearest ten square meters.

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Greatest Possible Error

Content:
So, we've seen how to calculate lower and upper bounds. Before we consider another example, note the following:

Content:
- The lower and upper bound depend on our approximation's degree of accuracy.
- In the last example, the degree of accuracy was [MATH: 10\,\textrm{cm}] because the rope was measured to the nearest [MATH: 10] centimeters.
- If we change the degree of accuracy, the lower and upper bounds will also change. So, for example, if we measured the rope to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{cm},] the lower and upper bounds would be different.
- The greatest possible error is the largest amount the "true" value can be from the approximation.
- This greatest possible error is always one-half of the degree of accuracy. So, in the last example, the greatest possible error in our measurement was

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{10\,\textrm{cm}}{2} = {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}}.]

Content:
We can use the greatest possible error to compute the lower and upper bounds quickly:

Content:
- To compute the lower bound of an approximation, we subtract the greatest possible error from the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have
[MATH: \textrm{lower bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} - {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 45\,\textrm{cm.}]
- To compute the upper bound of an approximation, we add the greatest possible error to the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have
[MATH: \textrm{upper bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} + {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 55\,\textrm{cm.}]

Item 3 — Example: Finding Bounds When Rounding to a Whole Number

Example Prompt:
The height [MATH: h] of a lamppost is [MATH: 30\,\textrm{ft}] to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ft}.] Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Our measurement is given to the nearest [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ft}.] So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

[MATH: \dfrac{1\,\textrm{ft}}{2} = 0.5\,\textrm{ft}.]

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

[MATH: lower bound|= 30ft − 0.5ft; = 29.5ft; upper bound|= 30ft + 0.5ft; = 30.5ft]

Since the exact value of [MATH: h] lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

[MATH: 29.5\,\textrm{ft} \leq h < 30.5\,\textrm{ft}.]

Item 6 — Example: Finding Bounds When Rounding to a Decimal Place

Example Prompt:
The area [MATH: a] of a golf course measures [MATH: 0.6\,\textrm{km}^2] to the nearest tenth of a square kilometer. Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Our measurement is given to the nearest [MATH: 0.1\,\textrm{km}^2.] So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

[MATH: \dfrac{0.1\,\textrm{km}^2}{2} = 0.05\,\textrm{km}^2.]

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

[MATH: lower bound|= 0.6km^{2} − 0.05km^{2}; = 0.55km^{2}; upper bound|= 0.6km^{2} + 0.05km^{2}; = 0.65km^{2}]

Since the exact value of [MATH: a] lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

[MATH: 0.55\,\textrm{km}^2 \leq a < 0.65\,\textrm{km}^2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Each dimension is given to the nearest [MATH: 10\,\textrm{m}.] So, the greatest possible error of these measurements is

[MATH: \dfrac{10\,\textrm{m}}{2} = 5\,\textrm{m}.]

We wish to find the upper bound for the area of the parking lot. Therefore, we require the upper bound of each dimension.

The upper bounds for each dimension are as follows:

[MATH: 90m + 5m = 95m; 50m + 5m = 55m]

So, the upper bound for the area of the parking lot is

[MATH: A|= 95m × 55m; = 5225; ≈ 5230m^{2},]

rounded to the nearest ten square meters.
